newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England delivers quarter point rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England delivers quarter point rate rise.

text.p: The Bank of England raised official interest rates to 6.75 percent from 6.50 percent on Thursday in a bid to cool consumer demand and meet the official inflation target.
This is the third rate rise in as many months and the second since the Bank was given the power to set interest rates.
The move followed a spate of data in the last month showing inflationary pressures building in the economy.

The quarter point increase had been widely predicted by City economists after last week's first budget by the new Labour government was seen as being not sufficiently tough to rein in consumer demand.
Speculation intensified this week that rates were heading higher after new data showed that the underlying inflation rate overshot the government's 2.5 percent target in June to stand at 2.7 percent.
But despite these expectations, the pound dropped over one pfennig against the German mark on the news.

Traders said the sharp fall was a result of disappointment that the rate rise was a only a quarter and not a half point. The pound soon found its feet to stand at 2.9630/40 marks compared with 2.9565 after the rate rise.

Government bonds gained modestly on the news. The September gilt future traded on the LIFFE exchange stood at 114-10 shortly just after the news, up 1/32 on the day compared with down 4/32 beforehand.
Shares pared early losses but remained in negative territory. The FTSE index of 100 leading shares stood at 4757.2, down 5.2 points on the day compared 4744 before the rate rise.

The Bank said the strength of the pound -- up over 20 percent against major currencies since last August -- complicated the rate decision but the recent run of strong economic data in the end forced its hand.

"The upward revision of estimated output growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 and recent development in monetary growth and retail sales indicated that a further tightening of monetary policy was necessary," the Bank said in a statement.

The government immediately backed the rate rise. In a statement released after the Bank's announcement, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said it was important that inflation be brought under control.

"Today the Bank of England has agreed with me that we must prevent a return to the boom-and-bust and that inflationary pressures in the economy which, despite persistent warning, the previous government negligently failed to tackle, must be brought under control."
